Subject: Service Center Staffing Review and Cost-Effective Assignment Plan

Overview
Our service center operates multiple service stations—front-line help desks, customer counters, and back-office departments—each with distinct customer demand patterns. We staff these stations with several types of employees whose skills and qualifications vary by station, and whose pace of work depends on the station they are assigned to.

Situation
- Customers arrive at each station at a known hourly rate, with volumes that differ across the center and throughout the day.
- Staff handle customers at different speeds depending on both their skill set and the specific station. Handling speed is tracked as the average minutes per customer.
- Not all staff types are qualified for all stations; some pairings are not permitted.
- Each staff type carries a different hourly cost, and the total number of available staff in each type is limited.

Staffing Challenge
The assignment problem requires choosing the right mix of staff across stations so that:
- Every station has sufficient coverage at all times.
- The combined throughput of assigned staff at each station stays comfortably ahead of incoming customer volume.
- Workloads are balanced so that people are not scheduled to be busy beyond the target fraction of their time.
- Only qualified staff are deployed to the stations they can support.
- The number of people scheduled in each staff category does not exceed what is available.

Key Requirements and Policies
- Service capacity versus demand: Because customer arrivals are tracked per hour while handling times are tracked in minutes per customer, we reconcile these units to compare each station’s expected demand with the team’s ability to process customers. The practical policy is to staff each station so the team’s combined pace remains safely ahead of expected arrivals, leaving room for variability, short breaks, and non-customer tasks.
- Utilization discipline: We will keep average on-duty time per person at or below a defined threshold. This helps prevent runaway queues, reduces burnout, and ensures responsiveness.
- Minimum coverage: Each station must have at least a baseline number of people at all times to guarantee service continuity, visibility, and safety.
- Qualifications and restrictions: Assignments that require certifications, systems access, or specialized training will be respected; unqualified pairings will not be scheduled.
- Resource limits: We will not schedule more individuals in a staff type than are actually available in that category.

Cost Objective
While meeting all of the above, our goal is to minimize total hourly staffing cost. In practice, this means placing lower-cost staff where they can meet performance standards, reserving higher-cost specialists for stations where they are most productive or uniquely required, and avoiding overstaffing by aligning capacity to demand with an appropriate buffer.

Expected Outcomes
- Stable service levels with shorter waits at busy stations.
- Balanced workloads that keep staff below the utilization cap.
- Compliance with coverage minimums and qualification rules.
- A transparent, defensible staffing plan that uses available resources efficiently and reduces total hourly cost.

Next Steps
Once the team reviews the operational data in the annex, we will produce a proposed station-by-station assignment for the target planning window, validate it with station leaders, and adjust for known events, training, and shift constraints. We will also highlight any stations where additional cross-training could unlock more flexible, lower-cost coverage in future cycles.
